column5: Divine self-identification at the bush
column6: At the same fire God identifies himself by name before Moses's mission; it directly accompanies the source context of Q20:14, where prayer and remembrance follow God's self-declaration.

column5: Approaching fire as holy ground
column6: Moses may not approach casually and must remove his sandals because the fire-side ground is holy, adding a concrete bodily response to the commentary's fire that becomes election and worship.

column5: Moses's staff for signs
column6: Moses receives the staff with which he will perform signs, supplying the Torah's concrete bridge from the bush commission to the commentary's staff-and-magicians scene.

column5: Elijah's prayer to the God of Abraham at a fire contest
column6: Elijah invokes the God of Abraham before the altar fire and asks that Israel know God and his servant; it joins fire, Abraham, divine name, and a public contest of allegiance.

column5: Fire consuming the offering
column6: The fire of YHWH falls on Elijah's offering, furnishing a Hebrew-Bible fire scene whose purpose is revelation and correction rather than the destruction of a condemned person.

column5: People fall on their faces and confess God
column6: After the fire the people prostrate themselves and confess YHWH as God, a close narrative meeting of fire, praise, and bowing with the commentary's magicians' prostration.

column5: Fire descends with divine glory
column6: At the temple dedication fire descends and God's glory fills the house, a further biblical scene in which fire marks divine presence rather than entry into punitive fire.

column5: Bowing and praise after the fire
column6: Seeing the fire and glory, Israel bows and gives thanks for God's enduring steadfast love; it closely combines the commentary's fire, praise, prostration, and permanence.

column5: Write a memorial in a book and rehearse it
column6: God tells Moses to write the event as a memorial in a book and place it in Joshua's hearing, directly joining Mosaic pages with remembrance and spoken teaching.

column5: Moses commanded to write covenant words
column6: Moses is told to write the covenant words, another explicit Torah source for the commentary's final appeal to earlier Mosaic pages.

column5: A written Torah copy read throughout life
column6: The king must write a Torah copy and keep it for continual reading and fear of God, a precise model of page, remembrance, obedience, and durable instruction.

column5: The Torah book kept as witness
column6: The written Torah is placed beside the ark as a witness, giving the commentary's named Mosaic pages a preserved and judicial function.

column5: Moses records the stages of the journey
column6: Moses writes Israel's journey-stages at God's command, meeting the commentary's scrolls with its fire-and-path movement.

column5: Book of remembrance for those who fear and esteem the name
column6: A book of remembrance is written for God-fearers who honor the divine name, tightly joining the commentary's reminder, fearer, name, and earlier pages.

column5: Words shut up and book sealed until the end
column6: Daniel is told to close the words and seal the book until the time of the end, a direct biblical combination of hidden end-time knowledge and written pages.

column5: Many purified and refined, while the wicked do not understand
column6: The end-time division has many made pure and refined while the wicked continue blindly; it closely meets the commentary's tazkiya, reminder, and divided response.

column5: Those guiding many to righteousness shine forever
column6: The wise shine and those who turn many to righteousness shine like stars forever, a biblical counterpart to guidance, high degrees, and lasting reward.

column5: Write the vision so a reader may run
column6: The vision is written plainly on tablets for a reader in motion, a specific meeting of the commentary's pages, public reminder, and path imagery.

column5: A vision for an appointed end that must be awaited
column6: The vision has an appointed time and may seem slow but will come, a close prophetic analogue to the commentary's concealed decisive hour.

column5: Word as lamp for foot and light for path
column6: The word gives a lamp and path-light, supplying a biblical verbal-light counterpart to the commentary's fire sought as guidance.

column5: Command as lamp and teaching as light on life's way
column6: The commandment is a lamp, teaching a light, and reproofs a way of life; it joins reminder, guidance, and life in terms specific to the commentary's movement.

column5: Walking through darkness by God's lamp
column6: Job recalls walking through darkness by God's shining lamp, a concrete light-and-way image alongside the commentary's fire sought for a guide.

column5: Prayer to the Father who sees in secret
column6: Jesus places prayer in the hidden room before the Father who sees in secret, directly combining the commentary's prayer-for-remembrance with its hidden divine knowledge.

column5: Nothing hidden from God's sight
column6: All creatures are exposed before the God to whom account is given, a direct Christian formulation for the commentary's God who knows what is open and concealed.

column5: Hidden things brought to light at judgment
column6: God will disclose hidden things of darkness and heart-motives, giving a judgmental sequel to the commentary's hidden matter and differentiated outcomes.

column5: No one can hide beyond God's sight
column6: The prophet asks whether anyone can hide in secret places from the God who fills heaven and earth, closely matching the commentary's claim of divine knowledge of the hidden.

column5: Hearing and doing words builds on rock
column6: The person who hears Jesus's words and does them is likened to a wise builder, a Christian response-to-reminder counterpart to the commentary's beneficial admonition.

column5: Rain and floods fail to overthrow the founded house
column6: Rain, flood, and wind strike the rock-founded house but it remains, directly meeting the commentary's flood and the contrast between what goes away and what remains.

column5: Hearing without doing builds on sand
column6: The hearer who does not act on the words builds on sand, providing a counterpart to the commentary's person who avoids the reminder.

column5: Flood destroys the house with no foundation
column6: Rain and floods bring a great fall to the sand-founded house, completing the commentary's water-borne testing and opposed human outcomes.

column5: Refined in the furnace of affliction
column6: God refines Israel in an affliction-furnace, an explicit prophetic development of the commentary's fire as corrective work rather than only punishment.

column5: A remnant refined by fire and calling God's name
column6: God brings a remnant through fire, refines it, and answers when it calls the divine name, closely coupling fire, purification, name, and responsive relationship.

column5: Fire consumes stubble because teaching is rejected
column6: Fire devours stubble and dry grass because people reject God's teaching, a very close prophetic fusion of dried vegetation, fire, and refusal of reminder.

column5: God's word like fire
column6: The divine word is likened to fire and a hammer, supporting the commentary's movement from recited reminder to a fire that actively corrects.

column5: God as consuming fire
column6: Hebrews names God a consuming fire in a worship context, a concise Christian meeting of the commentary's divine fire, awe, and praise.

column5: Saving someone by snatching them from fire
column6: Jude distinguishes rescuing people from fire from sharing their defilement, a concrete Christian complement to the commentary's concern with approaching versus entering fire.

column5: Wheat gathered and chaff burned with unquenchable fire
column6: The coming judge stores wheat but burns chaff, tightly combining the commentary's useful remainder, agricultural waste, human division, and great fire.

column5: Fruit-bearing branches pruned for greater fruit
column6: The grower prunes fruitful branches so they bear more fruit, supplying the corrective cultivation missing from the dried-and-burned branch image already developed by the commentary.

column5: Earth commanded to bring forth vegetation
column6: Creation begins with the earth bringing forth seed-bearing vegetation and fruit trees, an immediate Torah counterpart to the commentary's Creator bringing forth pasture.

column5: Rain, field growth, and a worker for the ground
column6: Before cultivated plants appear, the text notes both the absence of rain and of a human to work the soil, closely joining the commentary's rain, earth, body, and cultivated field.

column5: Seasonal rain producing land-yield and field fruit
column6: God's rain gives land its yield and trees their fruit, a covenantal counterpart to the commentary's rain-fed field and lasting useful produce.

column5: Teaching falling like rain on grass
column6: Moses compares teaching to rain, dew, and showers on tender grass, directly connecting the commentary's reminder to its water-and-pasture landscape.

column5: Growth like grass beside watercourses
column6: The renewed descendants spring up among grass like trees by water, a close prophetic image for the commentary's watered growth instead of dried refuse.

column5: Earth and garden making righteousness and praise sprout
column6: As earth makes sprouts grow, God makes righteousness and praise grow, joining the commentary's cultivated field to purification and praise.

column5: Created things wear out but salvation lasts forever
column6: Heavens vanish, earth wears out, and inhabitants die, while God's salvation and righteousness endure; this closely matches the commentary's temporary worldly life and better permanence.

column5: Arabic mar'a and Hebrew mir'eh for pasture
column6: Ezekiel depicts God feeding Israel in good pasture, Hebrew mir'eh, cognate with the commentary's Arabic mar'a; it turns the shared pasture image toward sustained divine shepherding.

column5: Arabic tazakka and Hebrew yizkeh around purity
column6: Job asks how a human, including one born of woman, can be pure, using Hebrew yizkeh from the z-k-y root cognate with the commentary's tazakka; its setting adds bodily finitude to purification.

column5: Arabic hayat and Hebrew hayyim in the command to choose life
column6: Beyond the existing choice motif, the Hebrew command choose hayyim and the commentary's hayat are cognate life terms; the verse grounds its life-choice in an explicit Semitic formulation.

column5: Praise offered with lips confessing God's name
column6: The community continually offers praise to God as the fruit of lips acknowledging the name, a direct Christian liturgical counterpart to the commentary's name, praise, and prayer.

column5: Prayers ascending as a memorial before God
column6: Cornelius's prayers and alms rise as a memorial before God, a specific Christian use of prayer and remembrance that complements the commentary's li-dhikri.

column5: Hope issuing in self-purification
column6: Those who hold the eschatological hope purify themselves, a compact Christian parallel to the commentary's purified person oriented toward the enduring future.

column5: Draw near, cleanse hands, and purify hearts
column6: James pairs drawing near to God with cleansing and a divided heart's purification, directly meeting the commentary's tazkiya and worshipful response.

column5: Holy ones of the Most High possess an everlasting kingdom
column6: The holy ones of the Most High receive and possess the kingdom forever, a direct biblical meeting of highestness, elevated status, and permanence.

column5: Everlasting kingdom given to the people of the Most High
column6: All dominions serve the holy people whose kingdom endures, answering the commentary's tyrant's temporary rule with lasting high rule under God.

column5: A ruler claims divinity and is answered that he is mortal
column6: The ruler of Tyre claims to sit as a god but is told he is human, a close prophetic counter-scene for the commentary's Pharaoh claiming supreme status.

column5: Hearing the word passes from death into life
column6: The one who hears and believes has eternal life and has crossed from death to life, a Christian response-to-reminder counterpart to the commentary's fire-bound non-life and purified alternative.

column5: Present goods reversed into future comfort and anguish
column6: Abraham contrasts the rich man's received good things in life with his later anguish and Lazarus's comfort, closely framing the commentary's worldly preference and later permanence.

column5: Broad way leading to destruction
column6: The broad gate and way end in destruction, providing a Christian path-and-outcome counterpart to the commentary's guidance, choice, and fire.

column5: Narrow way leading to life
column6: The difficult way leads to life and few find it, sharpening the commentary's sought guidance and its contrast between life-oriented response and loss.

column5: Future with death abolished
column6: Revelation's renewed world abolishes death, mourning, and pain; its eschatological endpoint gives a Christian counter-horizon to the commentary's fire where neither death nor life occurs.

column5: Righteous enjoying divine radiance in the world to come
column6: The Talmud's world-to-come scene gives the righteous crowns and enjoyment of divine radiance, a Jewish interpretive counterpart to enduring high degrees rather than temporary worldly life.

column5: God reveals a secret to prophetic servants
column6: Amos says God discloses the divine secret to prophets, a specific prophetic counterpart to the commentary's hidden matter becoming disclosed guidance.

column5: Melchizedek as priest of God Most High blessing Abraham
column6: The priestly blessing names God Most High in an Abraham scene, supplying the canonical context for the highness title already central to the commentary's first and last images.

column5: A name highly exalted above every name
column6: God highly exalts a name above every name, a Christian reapplication of name-and-highness that is relevant to the commentary's praise of the highest Lord but does not share its speaker.

column5: Every knee bends at the exalted name
column6: The universal bending of knees at the name gives a Christian liturgical analogue to the commentary's prostration and exalted name, with a different christological setting.

column5: Green marsh plant withering before other growth
column6: A water-dependent plant withers while still green, a specific wisdom image for the commentary's pasture turning into waste; the water setting differs from its valley flood.

column5: Floodwaters sweep away a false refuge
column6: Hail and overflowing waters expose a refuge made of falsehood, a prophetic water judgment that complements the commentary's flood separating what vanishes from what remains.

column5: Weeds gathered and burned at the age's end
column6: Jesus explains the weed-and-fire image as an end-time sorting, a necessary interpretive continuation of the field scene and the commentary's future fire.

column5: Righteous shining in their Father's kingdom
column6: The righteous shine in the kingdom after the furnace judgment, a Christian continuation that meets the commentary's high degrees and lasting reward.

column5: Abraham chosen to command his household in righteousness
column6: God says Abraham is known so that he will direct his household in God's way of righteousness and justice, adding a canonical Abrahamic election-and-teaching counterpart to the former-pages claim.

column5: Abraham's early rejection of idolatry
column6: These verses are commonly associated with young Abram's recognition of the earth's error in following carved images and his prayer for deliverance; exact wording and division should be verified, but the link is a specific Jewish precursor to the commentary's anti-idolatry Abraham.
